style: calm, natural hesitations, like explaining to a friend
slides: Now I want to talk a bit more about qualified writing. Or, as it's called in English, hedging.
How to say your claims at the right strength.
In general, I don't recommend memorizing endless lists of words and expressions for the essay.
What often happens is, students force in words and expressions they learned. Because, well, they learned them, so why not use them?
And that often causes semantic errors. Or at least an essay where the writing looks forced and fake.
So instead, I'll show you how to say things in a qualified way, at the level that fits academic writing... without any new or unusual words.
Let's look at a few examples.
Here's a sentence that's said as a fact.
The writer says, with no qualification at all, that if there's a ban on electric bicycles, the number of road accidents will definitely go down.
And there's a problem. We can't say for sure that this is what will happen.
For example, people who stop using electric bicycles might switch to some other vehicle that's more dangerous. Like, they'll move to motorcycles.
And then the number of road accidents won't necessarily go down.
So in short, the writer gives a guess, a hypothesis, without qualifying it, as if it were a fact. And that doesn't fit academic writing.
So think for a moment. How can we change the sentence to fix this? Take a moment.
Look, all we need is a small qualification.
Instead of 'will reduce', we can write 'may reduce'.
That doesn't say it will definitely reduce road accidents... but maybe it will.
And there you go. We took an absolute sentence, and qualified it.
Let's see another example.
Here we have two main problems. Take a moment, and try to find them both, and see how you'd fix them.
Okay, so let's see.
The first one is 'there is no doubt'. That's an absolute expression. It doesn't fit academic writing.
It's better to just drop it. That's it.
Most of the public will oppose the cameras. But now we get to the second problem.
The second problem is 'most of the public'.
When someone says 'most', he's actually saying that more than fifty percent of a certain group has some feature.
So here he's committing to the claim that more than half the public will oppose face-recognition cameras. How does he know that?
I mean, he probably didn't stop the essay, run outside, ask everyone in the country, get the results, and come back to finish writing... all in thirty-five minutes.
So he's saying something as a fact, but it isn't a fact. It might be true. But we don't know it.
And here I'll teach you a little trick that works really nicely. Instead of 'most', write 'many'.
How many is 'many'? Two or more. More than one.
What the sentence says didn't change. Whoever reads it thinks, okay, fair enough, many people really will oppose it.
But nobody can argue with me. Nobody can say this sentence is wrong.
So as a rule of thumb, if you don't know for sure that most of a group does or did something, don't use 'most'. Use 'many'.
You get almost the same effect... without taking a risk.
Let's see one more example.
And I ask... really? If there's no enforcement, every driver will do whatever he wants, and the roads will become a war zone?
Can't there be some drivers who'll keep obeying the law? And why? Because for them, it has nothing to do with enforcement.
They want to stay alive, so they drive by the law.
So again, we see a sentence that isn't qualified, and that doesn't fit academic writing.
Like before, take a moment, and try to think how to fix it.
Let's see how we can make this sentence a bit better, step by step.
We start by adding 'It is likely that' at the beginning of the sentence. That already qualifies the start.
So it's not 'without enforcement every driver will...'. It's 'It is likely that, without enforcement...'.
Next, 'every driver'. That's the second absolute expression. Remember the trick from before? Many.
So instead of 'every driver', 'many drivers'.
Now we have 'do whatever they want'. That's a bit of an everyday expression. It doesn't really fit academic writing.
So we replace it with, will not obey the law.
And look, I'm not searching for especially high words, to show off some unusual rich language.
No. I'm just trying to write clearly. Qualified, but clear.
Let's keep going. 'The roads will turn into a war zone.' Now that's real drama.
So of course, that expression doesn't fit academic writing either. The road isn't really going to turn into a war zone.
Instead, we can write, driving will become dangerous.
Let's see the whole thing. Before, and after.
Four changes. A qualified opening, 'many' instead of 'every', plain words instead of an everyday expression, and a calm claim instead of drama.
Same idea. Same position. But now nobody can say it's wrong.
Now, one warning. Qualified doesn't mean foggy.
Might, perhaps, possibly, could, in some ways, to some extent. That's six hedges on one small claim. And now the reader doesn't know what you're saying.
One qualifying word per claim is usually enough.
And your position itself stays clear. You qualify how sure you are about a result... you don't hide which side you're on.
Also, 'may' doesn't save a weak explanation. If the reason doesn't make sense, a hedge won't fix it. The explanation still has to work.
And there's no need to memorize lists. Just notice how you say things as you write. Is this certain? Is it everyone? Is it drama?
